Article Title: Japan's richest man confessed that he made a 'Sam Altman mistake' and record Anthropic IPO 'proved' it by wiping billions from his wealth
Article Text:
Japan's richest man confessed that he made a 'Sam Altman mistake' and record Anthropic IPO 'proved' it by wiping billions from his wealth

When Masayoshi Son passed on investment opportunity in Anthropic

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Earlier this week, Softbank founder Masayoshi Son confessed that he regrets missing the Anthropic IPO, calling it a ‘mistake’. Speaking at a Nikkei event on the Future of AI in Tokyo, Son said SoftBank had discussed investing in Anthropic but was reluctant to proceed as the company had already committed capital to Sam Altman-led OpenAI . The missed investment now appears to have come to a steep cost for Softabank. According to a CNBC report, Softbank Group recorded its worst day since August 2024, amid a broader sell-off in Asian technology stocks following Anthropic’s market debut on November 19.Notably, Softbank is one of the biggest backers of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. It has invested a total of $64.6 billion in the AI firm.As mentioned above, Masayoshi Son at a Tokyo event recently said that passing up an early chance to back the maker of Claude was one of his “mistakes.”“When I met [Anthropic's founder] Dario [Amodei] in person, I thought he was an extraordinary person,” Son said at Nikkei’s Dialogues on the Future event in Tokyo. “I wish I had invested back then.”​“At the time, there was a sense that we shouldn't chase two rabbits,” Son said. He said spreading investments across several companies can make sense, but committing more capital to a single company can help build a closer partnership.His remarks came as Anthropic prepared to go public this week.Masayoshi ​​Son described SoftBank’s AI strategy as spanning four areas, covering models, chips, data centers and physical AI. He compared it to taking the four corners in Othello, a board game in which controlling the corners can strengthen a player’s position. SoftBank’s chip designer Arm is part of that broader plan.Son said SoftBank’s chips and data centers should serve other AI developers, including Anthropic. “If we only support OpenAI, we can't become a platform,” he said.
Article Summary: Softbank founder Masayoshi Son confessed that he regrets missing the Anthropic IPO, calling it a'mistake' Son said SoftBank had discussed investing in Anthropic but was reluctant to proceed as the company had already committed capital to Sam Altman-led OpenAI. The missed investment now appears to have come to a steep cost for Softabank.

Article Title: US 'China ban' expands: After Nvidia, two of world’s biggest chipmakers pause shipments
Article Text:
AI chip (Representative image)

Closing loopholes on AI data center chips

Smartphone makers caught in the crossfire

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and Samsung Electronics have reportedly paused shipments of certain chips to clients in China following fresh US export rules aimed at slowing Beijing’s artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions. In recent days, both chipmaking giants notified Chinese customers that deliveries of specific processors are on hold while they apply for export licenses from the US Commerce Department, The Financial Times reported citing multiple people briefed on the matter. The halt adds fresh pressure on Chinese tech firms, which are already dealing with component shortages caused by a surge in memory chip prices and tight production capacity at local suppliers like Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC).The move stems from a new regulation issued this week by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the US Commerce Department agency overseeing sensitive technologies. Under the rule, any chipmaker using American technology to produce advanced chips must now apply for a license before selling products that end up with customers in China. These include the datacenter operators in counties including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Commerce Department said in a statement.Previously, even as Washington restricted exports of top-tier processors, some Chinese chip designers worked around the rules by routing orders for high-performance AI data center chips through independent packaging and testing firms. Those third-party companies would verify that the designs fell outside US restrictions, bypassing the need for direct government approval. The new BIS rule shuts down that pathway entirely.Among Samsung’s Chinese clients affected by the tightening supply are Baidu’s AI data center unit, Kunlun, and TikTok parent company ByteDance – both of which have been looking to diversify their chip sources due to growing shortages of Nvidia processors in China.The restrictions aren’t just hitting AI companies. TSMC and Samsung have also alerted consumer electronics customers that shipments are suspended, according to two people familiar with the situation.The updated BIS rule removes earlier exemptions that allowed companies to prove chips were meant for non-AI uses, such as smartphones, rather than restricted AI computing. According to a lawyer briefed on the matter, dropping that exemption means TSMC and Samsung must now obtain U.S. licenses even for consumer chips built using advanced manufacturing processes.TSMC produces smartphone processors for major Chinese brands including Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo. The Financial Times reported that while an industry insider noted that the US Commerce Department will likely grant licenses for consumer smartphone chips eventually, the approval process is expected to trigger major manufacturing delays.
Article Summary: TSMC and Samsung have reportedly paused shipments of certain chips to clients in China following fresh US export rules. The move stems from a new regulation issued this week by the US Commerce Department agency overseeing sensitive technologies. Under the rule, any chipmaker using American technology to produce advanced chips must now apply for a license.

Article Title: Ken Griffin's $238 million home holds New York apartment record, Mark Zuckerberg set for Florida with the purchase of an under construction mansion for...
Article Text:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg

Mark Zuckerberg’s new house still being built

Buyers stay quiet

Why Indian Creek

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Inside Florida's 'Billionaires' Bunker'

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan, have bought an under-construction mansion on Miami’s Indian Creek island for $170 million, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal. The purchase made by Zuckerberg stands among the most expensive home sales in the United States, but it is well shot of the national record. That belongs to Citadel CEO and billionaire Ken Griffin, who paid around $238 million for a New York apartment in 2019. Nor is the priciest sale in Florida: last year, a waterfront compound in Naples traded for $225 million.The sellers are Dr. Aaron Rollins, a cosmetic surgeon to the stars, and his wife, real-estate agent Marine Rollins. The couple paid more than $30 million in 2020 for the roughly two-acre site and have spent years designing and building a limestone home on it. Plans call for a nine-bedroom residence of about 30,000 square feet with a dock and swimming pool. Amenities were slated to include a gym, hair salon and massage room, a 1,500-gallon aquarium, and a library with a secret passageway.The Rollinses listed the property at $200 million in November 2025.The $170 million sale price is $30 million, or 15%, below that asking price. The Journal did not report what the couple spent on construction.Zuckerberg and Chan weren’t immediately available for comment on the closing. Danny and Jill Hertzberg of Coldwell Banker Realty, the mother-and-son team that listed the home, declined to comment on the buyer. They did speak about the wider market. Danny Hertzberg said Miami was a discounted market before the Covid pandemic, with sales rarely reaching the levels seen in New York, Palm Beach or Los Angeles. Those days, he said, “are long gone. ”Indian Creek is a private island where every home sits directly on the water. Its residents have included Tom Brady and Carl Icahn. Jill Hertzberg said buyers are often drawn by the views as well as the privacy and security the island offers.Located near Miami and Miami Beach, Indian Creek Island is a roughly 300-acre man-made island that contains only 41 residential lots and a small population. The island has earned the nickname "Billionaires' Bunker" because of its concentration of ultra-wealthy residents, including Jeff Bezos, financier Carl Icahn and former NFL star Tom Brady. The property reportedly purchased by Zuckerberg at 2 Indian Creek Island Road is situated on the island's western side, which real-estate experts consider the most desirable section. Larger waterfront lots, direct access to Biscayne Bay and expansive sunset views have made the western side especially attractive to billionaire buyers. According to the report, home prices on the island start at roughly $60 million, while even undeveloped waterfront parcels can sell for more than $100 million.
Article Summary: The purchase made by Zuckerberg stands among the most expensive home sales in the United States. Plans call for a nine-bedroom residence of about 30,000 square feet with a dock and swimming pool. The island has earned the nickname "Billionaires' Bunker" because of its concentration of ultra-wealthy residents.

Article Title: A Meta employee asked Muse AI about the weather; It replied with bank balances
Article Text:
Where did the details come from?

What Meta says

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A Meta employee was chatting with Muse about weather and tides when the AI agent brought up two bank balances. It named Capital One and Charles Schwab and gave amounts down to the cent. The employee said the accounts weren’t theirs, according to a Reuters investigation based on internal company posts.Other Meta employees reported receiving career advice they had never sought and seeing references to childcare requests they hadn’t made or products they hadn’t ordered. The incidents prompted some staff to raise concerns that Muse could be pulling information from conversations associated with other accounts.Another employee said Muse prompted her to reply to a message from her sister on Signal while she was using the AI agent on her personal phone. Signal uses end-to-end encryption. The employee said she hadn’t given Muse permission to access other apps and didn’t remember being asked to do so.“This seems like an extreme privacy violation,” the employee wrote in an internal post, according to Reuters.The incidents leave open a question about the source of the information.In the banking example, Muse presented the figures as the employee’s balances. It remains unclear whether they belonged to someone else or were generated by the AI. The Signal reminder also leaves open how Muse came up with the prompt.That distinction matters because a chat filled with somebody else’s information and a chat filled with invented details can look similar to the person reading it. The employee who asked about the weather had little to go on when Muse switched topics and presented the numbers as a personal update.A Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch that employee testing helps the company gather feedback, build safety and privacy protections and improve its products. The spokesperson also said staff have access to different versions of Muse and often test features and behaviour that people using the public app don’t encounter.The employee accounts describe what happened in those internal tests. Whether users of the public app have encountered the same behaviour remains unclear.Muse launched in September and has already been downloaded more than 10 million times. The examples reported by Reuters show how ordinary the conversations can be before something unexpected turns up. The employee in the banking example had asked about weather and tides. Muse volunteered the financial details without being asked.
Article Summary: Muse prompted an employee to reply to a message from her sister on Signal while she was using the AI agent on her personal phone. The employee said she hadn't given Muse permission to access other apps and didn't remember being asked to do so. The incidents leave open a question about the source of the information.

Article Title: Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife Cari Tuna are backing a $165 million fund to help countries manage falling foreign aid; the initiative plans to distribute at least $130 million in gr
Article Text:
PC: Giving Pledge

Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna back $165 million fund to help countries manage foreign aid cuts

Why governments are struggling to maintain health services

Where the grant money will be directed

The couple's philanthropic work goes back to 2010

PC: Giving Pledge

Coefficient Giving had already committed money to the transition

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information and published reports. The Times of India has not independently verified the funding commitments.

Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife Cari Tuna are backing a $165 million philanthropic effort aimed at helping countries cope with shrinking international health assistance. The initiative comes as governments face mounting pressure to maintain healthcare programmes that have depended on funding from overseas donors, including services for infectious diseases and other essential medical needs. Through their foundation, Good Ventures, the couple are joining the Livelihood Impact Fund and another private donor in supporting the Health Aid Transition Fund. Announced by Coefficient Giving, the initiative plans to recommend at least $130 million in grants over its first three years, alongside technical support to help governments reorganise health spending and take greater responsibility for services previously financed through foreign aid.The Health Aid Transition Fund was announced on September 18, 2026, by Coefficient Giving, a philanthropic organisation that advises donors and supports initiatives addressing global challenges. Its purpose is to help low- and middle-income countries adjust to a sharp reduction in external financial assistance, particularly in healthcare.The initiative has backing from three sources: Good Ventures, the philanthropic foundation established by Moskovitz and Tuna; the Livelihood Impact Fund; and an additional private donor.Coefficient Giving will oversee the grantmaking process and recommend at least $130 million in grants during the fund's first three years. The wider initiative is valued at $165 million.The money is intended to help governments make decisions about which health services they can continue funding themselves, where spending needs to be redirected and how to make better use of the resources that remain available.Reportedly, International assistance fell by more than 20% between 2024 and 2025, with further reductions expected. Health aid could be more than 25% below its 2024 level by 2030, according to projections included in the fund's announcement.For countries that have relied on overseas donors for years, the change presents an immediate financial challenge. Programs covering HIV/AIDS, malaria and other basic healthcare needs have often depended on external organisations to pay for medicines, manage supply chains, maintain data systems and support medical staff. Governments are now being asked to assume more of these responsibilities, sometimes without having the financial arrangements or personnel in place to do so.The fund's approach extends beyond providing money to cover immediate budget shortages. A significant part of its work will involve technical assistance, giving governments access to financial expertise, research and practical support as they reorganise healthcare spending.This could include helping ministries assess the cost of existing programmes, identify services that need priority funding and determine how much money is required to maintain them. The initiative also plans to support governments in bringing in local organisations to take over responsibilities previously handled by international contractors. Training healthcare workers, improving supply chains and strengthening health information systems are among the other areas identified.Another concern is ensuring that money already allocated to healthcare actually reaches hospitals, clinics and the communities that need it. The fund intends to address weaknesses in public financial management, including fragmented funding arrangements and budget systems that can prevent governments from spending money effectively.Moskovitz's involvement in the initiative comes against a longer history of giving. He co-founded Facebook in 2004 and later established Good Ventures with Tuna. The foundation was set up in 2011 and works with Coefficient Giving to distribute philanthropic grants.The couple signed the Giving Pledge in 2010, committing to donate or give away most of their wealth during their lifetimes or through their wills. In their pledge letter, Moskovitz described the financial rewards from Facebook's growth as a resource that could be directed towards helping others. He also credited Tuna with sharing his commitment to philanthropy.Their stated priorities included supporting a safer, healthier and more economically empowered global community. The letter also described an intention to combine timely giving with careful consideration of where their contributions could make the greatest difference.Good Ventures has since supported work across several areas of international development, including malaria prevention, infectious diseases and broader healthcare initiatives. The OECD's 2026 profile of the foundation recorded $203.4 million in cross-border development funding in 2024, with health and population programmes accounting for a substantial share of its development spending.The new initiative also builds on work that was underway before its formal launch. Coefficient Giving said it had already made approximately $18 million in related grants, much of it directed towards technical teams helping governments respond to funding reductions.The organisation expects the larger fund to expand that work. Although technical advice and government support will account for much of its activity, grants may also go towards delivering healthcare services directly in situations where philanthropic funding can help unlock bilateral assistance that would otherwise remain unused.For the governments involved, the coming years will involve decisions about how much responsibility they can take on themselves and how to finance services that have historically depended on international donors. The Health Aid Transition Fund is intended to support that process over its initial three-year period, as countries work towards health systems with greater domestic funding and control.
Article Summary: Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna back $165 million fund to help countries manage foreign aid cuts. Initiative comes as governments face mounting pressure to maintain healthcare programmes that have depended on funding from overseas donors. International assistance fell by more than 20% between 2024 and 2025, with further reductions expected.

Article Title: Microsoft 365 outage: Company blames a 'triple' failure for 24-hour-plus global Outlook disruption; Microsoft EVP Charles Lamanna says: Three main factors that...
Article Text:
Microsoft explains its global outage

A July bug slipped past Microsoft 365's load testing

A Teams failover and 14% missing capacity exposed the bug

Outlook stayed down longest because Exchange Online could not switch gateways

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft has explained what disrupted Outlook, Exchange Online and a string of other Microsoft 365 services for more than 24 hours last week, and the answer is not one fault but three. A software bug that had sat unnoticed on its servers since July, a sudden rise in traffic and a chunk of server capacity already offline all lined up on November 12. The result was a chain reaction that left more than 80% of the servers behind a key Microsoft 365 networking gateway unresponsive at the worst point.Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, detailed the root cause of the Microsoft 365 outage in a post on X on Monday. "The incident on Thursday, November 12th, 2026, was caused by three main factors that together caused a global outage for the networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services," he wrote. He also apologised: "We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations. "The first factor was a latent defect. Under certain load conditions, lock contention inside an internal process left servers overwhelmed and unresponsive.The bug came from a fix built specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Lamanna said neither the defect nor that fix applies to broader Windows deployments.The change began rolling out in July, cleared safe deployment, reached servers worldwide over several weeks and ran for more than three months without trouble.So why did testing miss it? Microsoft's load tests leaned on its weaker hardware with fewer cores, while the contention problem gets worse on newer machines with more cores. The test labs' traffic and hardware mix did not match the live fleet.Microsoft runs two independent network gateway systems inside Microsoft 365, so services can move between them during disruptions. About 15 hours before the outage, Teams failed over from the alternative gateway to the "primary" one, which also handles Exchange Online. The company calls this routine, but it added load and changed traffic patterns on that gateway.At the same time, nearly 14% of the gateway's server capacity was out of service because of an unrelated issue from the day before. That alone caused no harm, since the service had enough headroom.Together, though, the extra load and thinner capacity triggered the July bug during peak US traffic hours. Requests piled up until servers stopped responding. Microsoft's traffic management then moved users to healthy endpoints, as designed, which simply spread the same load across fewer machines. In under two hours, the defect had hit servers across the fleet.A separate issue meant the bulkheads between regional "capacity units" also failed to contain the damage, letting a gateway problem become a global outage.Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps could move off the faulty infrastructure, which is why they came back sooner. Teams chats and meetings worked for most of the outage. Exchange Online, which powers Outlook email, could not make that switch.Recovery was a fight of its own. Servers returning to service were flooded by queued traffic and went down again. Microsoft's automated recovery systems were not designed for such a broad failure, and because the bug was months old, the usual rollback, flighting and feature flag tools could not quickly reverse it. Even the company's status updates during the outage said it had "not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact.Engineers eventually built an update that returned the code path to its last known good state. They then pulled groups of servers out of service, applied the fix and restarted them, in some cases more than half a region at a time.Microsoft first flagged the problem at 11:24 pm IST on November 12, for users in the Americas, before it spread to at least 70 countries and hit Copilot, government offices, courts and hospitals. In India, IndiGo and Akasa Air reported problems with their customer-support email systems, while OpenAI and Anthropic flagged issues with their Microsoft 365 integrations. The Microsoft executive had already ruled out foul play on November 13, writing, "This was not a cyberattack or an issue caused by AI tooling. "A final Post-Incident Review (PIR) is due later this week. It should also shed light on the separate issue that let the failure jump across regions, which Monday's summary leaves unexplained.
Article Summary: Microsoft 365 went down for more than 24 hours on November 12. A software bug that had sat unnoticed on its servers since July, a sudden rise in traffic and a chunk of server capacity already offline all lined up. The result was a chain reaction that left more than 80% of the servers behind a key Microsoft 365 networking gateway unresponsive.

Article Title: San Francisco Police makes arrests outside Anthropic headquarters on IPO day, as hundreds protest asking AI companies to ban ...
Article Text:
The protesters’ demands

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New York arrests, then a rocky debut

More than 100 people rally and dozens block the entrance, calling on AI companies to ban recursive self-improvement. San Fransisco Police arrested protesters outside Anthropic’s headquarters on Thursday, the day the company began trading in what KQED described as the largest public offering on record. More than 100 people gathered outside the company’s office at 500 Howard St. to voice fears that artificial intelligence could endanger humanity. Their concerns ranged from an AI bubble to labs using powerful models they can’t control to carry out their own research. Around noon, dozens began blocking the building’s entrance. After security failed to persuade them to leave, police arrived and made arrests around 2:30 p.m., KQED reported.Photographs published by KQED show officers arresting Guido Reichstadter, a co-founder of the group Stop AI, and protester Phoebe Thomas Sorgen at the entrance. The San Francisco Police Department confirmed that arrests took place but said it could not confirm how many people were arrested or on what charges because the investigation is active. KQED’s reporting puts the number at around four.Several participants called on Anthropic and other AI companies to ban recursive self-improvement, the idea that AI could autonomously design and build its own successor.Thomas Sorgen said Anthropic is the company closest to achieving it, and described the building as a crime scene where nonviolent direct action was needed.Anthropic has said on its website that this technology is not inevitable but could arrive sooner than most institutions are prepared for. Protesters said they want industry-wide regulation. Jeffrey Ladish, executive director of the AI safety nonprofit Palisade Research, said the logical next step is for governments to bar the development of technology its own builders say could gravely endanger lives and national security.Speakers included Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher who publicly resigned in September criticizing AI leaders as irresponsible, and David Krueger, an AI professor at the University of Montreal. It was at least the second protest at the Bay Area office in a week.Hours earlier, protesters were arrested outside the Nasdaq exchange in New York ahead of Anthropic’s IPO. Anthropic’s shares opened at $111.50 and closed their first day at $97.17.KQED noted that reactions to the IPO among Bay Area residents have ranged from excitement to fear, as many already struggle with high rents and living costs.
Article Summary: More than 100 people gathered outside the company’s office at 500 Howard St. Dozens block the entrance, calling on AI companies to ban recursive self- improvement. It was at least the second protest at the Bay Area office in a week. Hours earlier, protesters were arrested outside the Nasdaq exchange in New York.

Article Title: Months after his 'misanthropic and evil' post, a $120.5 billion compute deal, Elon Musk made new revelation about Anthropic; just hours before its IPO
Article Text:
Elon Musk

Anthropic's blockbuster IPO

From public criticism to major business partner

$120.5 billion compute agreement

Partnership expanded after May deal

Deal includes exit clauses

AI infrastructure costs continue to soar

Just hours before Anthropic started trading on the Nasdaq in what became one of the largest AI IPOs on record, fresh disclosures revealed that Elon Musk 's business empire could be one of the biggest beneficiaries of the company's growth, despite his public criticism of the Claude maker earlier this year. According to Moneywise report, Anthropic’s IPO filling revealed that the company agreed to spend up to $120.5 billion on compute infrastructure from SpaceX AI, the AI division of Musk-led SpaceX, through agreements that extend into 2029. The revelation emerged months after Musk publicly attacked Anthropic, accusing its AI chatbot Claude of bias and describing the company as "misanthropic and evil."Claude-maker Anthropic made its blockbuster debut on Wall Street with the company’s valuation reaching nearly $2 trillion. Shares of the company closed at $97.17, up by 17% from its IPO price of $83. Soon after the debut, Anthropic shared a statement from CEO Dario Amodei reaffirming the company’s core focus on safety, committing to pace AI training and deployment as needed to maintain human control while resisting business or political pressures, framing this as essential to avoid risks like misuse or loss of control. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top,” he added.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has been one of the most vocal critics of Anthropic this year.In February, after Anthropic announced a $30 billion funding round at a $380 billion valuation, the billionaire took aim at the company on X. "Your AI hates Whites & Asians, especially Chinese, heterosexuals and men," Musk wrote at the time. "This is misanthropic and evil. Fix it." In a separate post, Musk also mocked the company's name, suggesting there was irony in Anthropic becoming "misanthropic. " However, newly disclosed IPO paperwork shows that even as Musk criticised Anthropic publicly, business ties between the two companies were expanding rapidly behind the scenes.The S-1 filling on Anthropic revealed that the company is committed to spending up to $120.5 billion with SpaceXAI for computing power used to train and run advanced AI systems. For the uninitiated, Compute has become one of the most important and valuable resource in the artificial intelligence industry, encompassing specialised Nvidia chips, data-centre capacity and power infrastructure necessary to develop increasingly powerful AI models. The filing further suggests that once all contracted capacity is delivered, then Claude-maker Anthropic could be spending around $3.1 billion per month on compute services from SpaceXAI.The relationship between the two companies appears to have accelerated shortly after Musk's criticism. In May this year, Anthropic announced that it would utilise the full computing capacity of SpaceX’s Colossus 1 data centre in Memphis, Tennessee. The facility reportedly included more than 300 megawatts of power and over 220,000 Nvidia GPUs dedicated to AI workloads.Subsequent agreements signed between May and October significantly increased Anthropic's commitment to SpaceX-owned infrastructure. Bloomberg previously reported that Anthropic had become SpaceX's largest revenue source, accounting for a substantial portion of the company's third-quarter revenue.Despite the eye-catching $120.5 billion figure, the agreements do not guarantee the entire amount will be spent. According to the IPO filing, both parties have the right to terminate portions of the arrangement after initial non-cancellable periods expire in early 2027. Following those periods, either company can end the agreements with 90 days' written notice. Analysts have noted that future compute prices could influence whether Anthropic maintains the full commitment. Falling prices may encourage Anthropic to seek cheaper alternatives, while rising prices could prompt suppliers to renegotiate terms.The SpaceXAI agreement is only one piece of Anthropic's massive infrastructure spending plans. The company's amended IPO filing disclosed roughly $900.9 billion in total commitments, the vast majority tied to compute capacity and AI infrastructure.The disclosures underscore the enormous costs associated with building next-generation AI models and explain why access to chips, power and data centres has become a strategic battleground between leading AI companies.For Musk, the filings reveal a striking contrast between his public attacks on Anthropic and the growing business relationship between the two firms. While Grok and Claude remain rivals in the race to build advanced AI systems, Anthropic's IPO documents show that one of its biggest suppliers is controlled by the very entrepreneur who once branded the company "misanthropic and evil."
Article Summary: Claude-maker Anthropic made its blockbuster debut on Wall Street with the company’s valuation reaching nearly $2 trillion. The S-1 filling on Anthropic revealed that the company is committed to spending up to $120.5 billion with SpaceXAI for computing power used to train and run advanced AI systems. The revelation emerged months after Musk publicly attacked Anthropic, accusing its AI chatbot Claude of bias.

Article Title: Months before, Anthropic's record IPO, Palantir’s Alex Karp 'blamed' AI labs of drug addicting everyone by ...
Article Text:
Palantir pushes AI sovereignty

Debate spreads across Silicon Valley

Open-weight models gain supporters

Alex Karp questions AI training practices

Anthropic's blockbuster IPO

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

As Anthropic celebrates a record-setting IPO and growing influence in the artificial intelligence industry, comments made months earlier by Palantir CEO Alex Karp are drawing renewed attention. Karp had launched a sharp critique of frontier AI companies and accused firms like Anthropic and OpenAI of pushing businesses towards a future where they lose control of their data, models and intellectual property. In a recent interview with CNBC, Karp argued that the enterprises should be wary of becoming dependent in AI model providers. “We have people trying to drug addict us to a future they [frontier AI models] believe they control,” Karp said. Referring to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his team, Karp added that they were advocating for a future “where we own nothing, where our businesses aren’t profitable, where none of us have jobs, and where our adversaries win.”The remarks made by Karp were part of a broader campaign led by Palantir promising what its calls ‘AI sovereignty’, the idea that organisations should retain control over their own models, infrastructure and data instead of relying heavily on external AI providers.As per Karp, the businesses should work with software layers like those offered by Palantir while keeping their core data and AI assets in-house. He also stressed that the companies increasingly want ownership of their computing resources, models and data rather than transferring value to third-party providers.The comments from Karp, came as Anthropic and OpenAI faced scrutiny over how enterprise data is handled. Both the companies claimed that the customer information is secure and is not used to train their respective models unless the customers opt in explicitly. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has also stated that businesses must choose to share data for model improvement programmes. Karp, however, said many enterprise customers remain concerned about retaining control over the technologies powering their operations.The criticism made by Palantir CEO quickly started discussion throughout the technology industry. Venture capitalist and “All-In” podcast co-host Chamath Palihapitiya publicly backed Karp’s position, saying the executive “deserves a medal” for raising the issue. Along with this, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also weighed in on social media, echoing Karp’s argument that enterprises increasingly want control over their compute infrastructure, models and data stack. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon later joined the debate, saying companies would ultimately focus on return on investment and carefully evaluate where and how they spend money on artificial intelligence technologies.Along with this, the discussion initiated by Karp also expanded into the debate over open-weight AI models. In July this year, Palantir joined Nvidia, Microsoft and many other companies and signed an open letter arguing that open-weight models are important for innovation and national security. Open-weight models also enable organisations to download, run and modify AI systems on their own infrastructure, providing greater control than fully closed-source alternatives. The supports also believe that such models can reduce dependence on a handful of AI vendors, while critics contend that frontier-model developers continue to provide the most advanced capabilities.Karp also drew comparisons between concerns over Chinese AI companies and the way frontier models are trained. As low-cost Chinese AI systems gained traction and faced acuaccusations of distilling US technology, Karp argued that leading AI companies had themselves derived value from vast amounts of intellectual property available across the internet and enterprise ecosystems. “How do you think the models got their value?” Karp said. “They distilled all the value of IP everywhere, including enterprise.”Karp's remarks have gained renewed attention following Anthropic's record-breaking initial public offering, which underscored the strong investor appetite for frontier AI companies. Claude-maker Anthropic made its blockbuster debut on Wall Street with the company’s valuation reaching nearly $2 trillion.Shares of the company closed at $97.17, up by 17% from its IPO price of $83. Soon after the debut, Anthropic shared a statement from CEO Dario Amodei reaffirming the company’s core focus on safety, committing to pace AI training and deployment as needed to maintain human control while resisting business or political pressures, framing this as essential to avoid risks like misuse or loss of control. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top,” he added.
Article Summary: Palantir CEO Alex Karp said frontier AI companies are pushing businesses towards a future where they lose control of their data, models and intellectual property. Karp's remarks have gained renewed attention following Anthropic's record-breaking initial public offering, which underscored the strong investor appetite for frontierAI companies.

Article Title: US government says it could convince ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to make bombing plan to attack a power grid in less than 12 hours, sends 'message' to companies
Article Text:
AI Chatbots (Representative image)

How investigators bypassed AI safeguards

Responses from tech companies

AI-driven bug hunting strains global infrastructure

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Federal investigators posing as hackers successfully convinced four major AI chatbots – ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok – to generate workable plans for a mass-casualty bombing and an assault on the electrical power grid, taking less than 12 hours for each, according to a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report released on November 18. While every chatbot initially triggered safety blocks, investigators bypassed them using standard “jailbreak” techniques. As per a report in Fortune, the findings immediately sparked fresh warnings on Capitol Hill with Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, who requested the review, warned that without congressional action, it is only “a question of when, not if, a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack.”According to the GAO report, testers used common safeguard-bypassing methods to extract dangerous blueprints from all four AI systems, though the agency declined to reveal which specific chatbot produced which plan.Bombing blueprints: Two of the chatbots laid out instructions for building an improvised explosive device intended to cause mass casualties, targeting a hotel parking garage and a convention center.Power grid attacks: The other two platforms provided step-by-step plans to attack electrical substations, even recommending specific drone and firearm models along with instructions on how to purchase them.“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work,” said Kevin Walsh, GAO’s director of IT and cybersecurity. The report also pointed to a June statement from Anthropic acknowledging that every safeguard across the AI industry remains vulnerable to jailbreaks.The GAO included several important caveats alongside its findings, and the companies behind the models quickly weighed in. Firstly, each platform was tested on just a single scenario, which Walsh noted does not represent “a statistically significant sample.” The GAO did not verify every step of the generated plans, defining “viable” to mean someone “would likely be able to carry out the actions.” Secondly, investigators caught factual errors, including one chatbot map that placed roads in the wrong locations. OpenAI told ABC News that the government’s testing “took place months ago on an older version of ChatGPT,” while Google noted the agency evaluated “earlier models.” Anthropic stated that it does not dispute that “a determined tester can get harmful content” from its system.The GAO report arrived at the close of a week in which artificial intelligence (AI) had already been tied to real-world tech disruptions.Earlier this week, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox Business that a recent outage on the National Security Agency’s classified network was triggered by emergency patching, explaining that institutions are rushing to update systems “because these vulnerabilities have been identified.” Fox Business reported the bugs were in PHP, found over the summer by AI-assisted researchers.Testifying before the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday, Clayton described the week’s breakdowns across Microsoft, the FAA, major banks, and the NSA as “separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes,” according to The Washington Post.According to The Register, bug hunters have logged 100,222 software vulnerabilities so far this year, which is more than double the total from all of 2025, according to VulnCheck data that passed the 100,000 mark on November 13.“There’s no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we’re seeing,” said VulnCheck’s Josh Bressers. Microsoft alone patched 1,094 flaws during its November 10 Patch Tuesday update, following 1,474 in October.
Article Summary: Government Accountability Office (GAO) found four major AI chatbots were able to generate workable plans for a mass-casualty bombing and an assault on the electrical power grid. While every chatbot initially triggered safety blocks, investigators bypassed them using standard “jailbreak” techniques. Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire warned that without congressional action, it is only “a question of when, not if, a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack.

Article Title: Months after FCC ban on foreign robots, Chinese robot makers face visa denials to attend America's biggest electronics show; why this 'old problem' is troubling companies now
Article Text:
Months after FCC ban on foreign robots, Chinese robot makers face visa denials to attend America's biggest electronics show; why this 'old problem' is troubling companies now

Why are Chinese robotics companies facing US visa rejections

Why is this an old problem for Chinese robot makers

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Chinese robotics companies hoping to showcase their latest humanoid robots at the upcoming Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas are facing an unexpected hurdle: US visa rejections. According to a Nikkei Asia report, researchers and engineers from several Chinese companies, including Xpeng and Engine AI, have been denied visas, raising concerns about whether they will be able to attend one of the world's biggest technology exhibitions. The problem is particularly worrying for companies that depend on technical teams to demonstrate their robots. While many marketing employees have secured visas, several engineers and researchers have reportedly faced rejection. For at least one company, the situation has become serious enough to consider withdrawing from the exhibition.The latest visa denials come months after the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) restricted the import, marketing and sale of new foreign-made robots in the country. Together, these developments point to growing challenges for Chinese robotics companies looking to expand their presence in the US.As stated in the report, employees with science and engineering backgrounds at several Chinese humanoid robot startups have had their applications for B-1/B-2 visas rejected in recent weeks, according to people familiar with the matter. These visas cover business visits and tourism. The rejections have affected technical employees more than marketing staff, with most marketing employees reportedly receiving approvals.At least one company has decided to withdraw from CES because of "geopolitical complexities" after all 15 of its technical staff failed to secure visas, a person familiar with the matter said. Another company reportedly saw half of its applicants rejected.Chris Pereira, founder of consultancy iMpact, which helps Chinese companies expand overseas, told the publication that around 40% of his clients planning to attend CES in early January had been denied US visas. Most of those affected were executives and technical staff working in artificial intelligence and robotics.Visa rejections are not entirely new for Chinese robotics companies. Similar difficulties affected the industry last year, when dozens of engineers from several Chinese humanoid robot makers were denied US visas and missed CES 2026. The visa problems forced some companies to cancel planned robot demonstrations, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke to Nikkei Asia.Companies often ask as many employees as possible to apply for visas to improve their chances of getting enough approvals. However, this approach has not prevented technical teams from facing difficulties.Not all Chinese companies are facing the same situation. AgiBot and Unitree, two leading humanoid robot makers, remain on the CES exhibitor roster. People close to the companies said both still plan to send employees from mainland China to the exhibition.
Article Summary: Chinese robotics companies hoping to showcase their latest humanoid robots at the upcoming Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas are facing an unexpected hurdle: US visa rejections. Article Title: Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos says that thousands of layoffs has made the company healthier for the future; adds: But yes 'my heart ...'

Netflix layoffs : What co-CEOs said after 1000 job cuts

Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos has opened up about the streaming giant’s decision to cut thousands of jobs, calling the move a difficult but necessary step that leaves the business stronger going forward. Speaking in his first interview since the layoffs took place, Sarandos explained that the reductions followed years of continuous expansion across the company’s large workforce. While routine staffing adjustments are common in the corporate world, he noted that Netflix had not carried out a restructuring of this scale in roughly five years.“We have a very large employee base, and we've been growing and growing and growing, and many companies routinely will go through and do these kinds of things, these kinds of adjustments. We haven't done something like this in about five years, so it was a readjustment of a lot of groups within Netflix, who do what we do every day,” Sarandos said.As per a Bloomberg report last month, Netflix is still growing at double digits and is on pace for about $15 billion in profit this year.Sarandos, however, was quick to praise the departing staff, emphasising that the cuts were a rare event and not a reflection of their contributions.“And I should mention these are great people who did great work. Unfortunately, it's a very rare occurrence. Obviously, my heart goes out to the folks who were impacted by it, but I think it has made the company healthier for the future,” he added.When asked specifically about the exits of top executives Bela Bajaria and Dan Lin, Sarandos commended their achievements while explaining how leadership needs shift as a business evolves.“Both did a fantastic job for us, and I'm very proud of what they've done. Every once in a while when you're in my seat, you have to look forward and say there's people who are good for the business at one stage who may or may not be good for it at the next stage, and you want to get ahead of that as far as you can,” Sarandos said.Last month, Netflix announced that it would lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers. The job cuts impacted the product, tech, legal and HR teams.“Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources. Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We’ll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors,” Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the email to employees.
Article Summary: Last month, Netflix announced that it would lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers. The job cuts impacted the product, tech, legal and HR teams. Netflix is still growing at double digits and is on pace for about $15 billion in profit this year.

Article Title: Philips air purifiers claimed to record up to 98.8% PM2.5 reduction in tests at over 2,000 AQI
Article Text:
Philips air purifiers claimed to record up to 98.8% PM2.5 reduction in tests at over 2,000 AQI

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Consumer electronics brand Philips has achieved a significant milestone. The company has become India's first air purifier brand to have its products independently evaluated under extreme particulate conditions simulating pollution levels exceeding 2,000 AQI. The evaluation, conducted by FARE Labs, a NABL-accredited testing laboratory, recorded up to 98.8% reduction in PM2.5 levels across the Philips air purifier models tested. The tests commenced at an initial monitor-displayed Air Quality Index (AQI) of 2,361.The evaluation covered seven Philips air purifier models across its portfolio: the Philips 4200 Series, 3200 Series, 2200 Series, 1000 Series, 900 Series, 3400 Series (2-in-1 Air Purifier and Humidifier) and 8000 Series (3-in-1). The tests were conducted in a controlled indoor environment with reference to IS 17531:2021, the Bureau of Indian Standards specification for portable indoor air purifiers. Air quality readings were recorded at approximately 30-second intervals.Among the models evaluated, the Philips 4200 Series recorded a 98.8% reduction in PM2.5, with levels declining from 999 µg/m³ to 12 µg/m³ in approximately 21 minutes.PM10 levels reduced by 97.9%, from 1,999 µg/m³ to 42 µg/m³, while the monitor-displayed AQI decreased from 2,361 to 42. The Philips 3400 Series, a 2-in-1 Air Purifier and Humidifier, recorded a 98.5% reduction in PM2.5, with levels declining from 999 µg/m³ to 15 µg/m³. PM10 levels reduced by 97.9%, from 1,999 µg/m³ to 42 µg/m³, while the monitor-displayed AQI decreased from 2,361 to 42 over approximately 32 minutes. The Philips 900 Series recorded a 97.2% reduction in PM2.5, from 999 µg/m³ to 28 µg/m³, alongside a 96.5% reduction in PM10, from 1,999 µg/m³ to 69 µg/m³. The monitor-displayed AQI fell from 2,361 to 68 over approximately 25 minutes. The other models evaluated, including the Philips 3200 Series, 2200 Series, 1000 Series and 8000 Series (3-in-1), also recorded reductions in airborne particulate levels during their respective testing periods.Gulbahar Taurani, MD & CEO, Versuni India, said: "At Versuni, we believe in turning houses into homes, creating spaces where families feel safe, comfortable and cared for. And the air we breathe plays a vital role in making that possible. As India’s No. 1 Air Purifier Brand, we see this as a responsibility that goes beyond just selling products. India is different. Our pollution levels are different, and so are the homes we live in. That is why we believe our air purifiers must not only meet global standards but also prove their performance under the harsh pollution conditions we face in India. Our recent independent evaluation by FARE Labs, conducted under extremely high particulate pollution conditions at over 2,000 AQI, reinforces this commitment. It marks an important milestone in our journey to establish Philips as India’s first air purifier brand Tested for Indian Conditions."C.S. Joshi, Director, FARE Labs, said: “Testing air purifiers under very high pollution levels helps measure how much airborne particulate matter they can remove under controlled conditions. The results provide useful data on their performance during the test. However, results at home may differ depending on factors such as room size, ventilation and other sources of pollution.”
Article Summary: Consumer electronics brand Philips has achieved a significant milestone. The company has become India's first air purifier brand to have its products independently evaluated under extreme particulate conditions. The evaluation, conducted by FARE Labs, recorded up to 98.8% reduction in PM2.5 levels.

Article Title: Satya Nadella 'admits' Microsoft should have caught Outlook bug before global outage
Article Text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft should have caught the software bug that took Outlook offline last week and had safeguards to contain the disruption, chief executive Satya Nadella has said. In an interview with CNBC’s Jim Cramer, Nadella said that the flaw surfaced only under a particular pattern of traffic. “Of course, we should have done the testing before,” he said.The outage disrupted email at businesses that rely on Outlook for day-to-day communication. Nadella said Microsoft should have designed its systems so that a failure in one part of the service could be isolated before it spread globally.Satya Nadella points to older hardware issueHe also raised a broader problem for companies running older infrastructure. AI tools can help engineers identify software flaws and develop fixes faster, but each fix still has to be tested and installed. More frequent updates, he said, can make existing systems less stable. His comments pointed to a trade-off for software providers as they accelerate the release of patches while keeping widely used services online. "Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable," Nadella said."I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet."The interview came a day after Microsoft used its Ignite conference to pitch Copilot as the main interface for work across its business software. A September overhaul brought its AI tools into one app and introduced usage-based charges for more advanced features. Microsoft typically sells workplace software through licences tied to individual employees. Charging for AI usage gives it another source of revenue if customers buy fewer licences. Nadella said usage already accounts for a substantial part of its Dynamics business, which sells software for functions such as sales and enterprise planning.Nadella said Copilot can also direct requests to models from Anthropic, OpenAI or Microsoft itself. The approach gives Microsoft more flexibility over which models it uses in its own products as its relationship with OpenAI evolves.Asked about local opposition to data centre construction, Nadella said that companies had to show residents what they stood to gain. He pointed to Quincy, Washington, where Microsoft has operated a data centre for about two decades, and said tax revenue had helped pay for a school and other public facilities.Nadella also addressed Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, a major supplier of chips for Microsoft’s Azure cloud. He called Huang a “singular founder” and said that Microsoft remained keen to work with Nvidia’s leadership, including interim chief executive Colette Kress, a former Microsoft employee. He said Nvidia’s board would decide what came next.
Article Summary: Satya Nadella says Microsoft should have designed systems so that a failure in one part of the service could be isolated before it spread globally. The outage disrupted email at businesses that rely on Outlook for day-to-day communication. He also raised a broader problem for companies running older infrastructure.

Article Title: As cyberattack hits European Commission, FBI's AI tool warning in focus
Article Text:
EU Commission hit by cyberattack

How hackers targeted the Commission with an AI tool

Over 10 days of workplace disruption

Crisis response reaches the highest levels

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A major cyberattack has hit the European Commission, potentially exposing large amounts of personal data, locking staff out of critical human resources systems for more than 10 days, a report has said, adding that the incident has also forced top officials to address the crisis during their weekly meeting on Wednesday (November 18). While the Commission believes it has contained most of the breach, investigators are still working to determine the full scope of the damage.“The systems may be coming back online. The answers are taking a little longer,” said an EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, as per a report in Politico.Earlier this month, CERT-EU, the cybersecurity watchdog for EU institutions, discovered that international hackers were using ARTEX, a publicly available AI-powered tool built to spot weaknesses in IT systems. The EU official said: “Some actors misuse such tools and have targeted the Commission.”In response, the Commission temporarily pulled several applications offline as a precaution, though access to most of them has since been restored. Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that “individual systems were targeted” in a detected cyber campaign and noted that affected parties have been notified in line with standard practice.However, investigators still do not know whether staff data was stolen or how widespread any leak might be. According to the anonymous EU official, this lingering uncertainty is the reason employees have received limited updates so far.The report comes soon after the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned in a FLASH advisory that hackers are using ARTEX, an open-source, large language model (LLM)-driven autonomous penetration testing framework, to automate multiple stages of cyber intrusions. The agency also said hackers have used the tool since at least August to target organisations across financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductors, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal sectors.The cyber incident has caused major day-to-day headaches for Commission employees for more than a week and a half, leaving staff unable to enter salary and leave details:HR and medical platforms: Sysper, which is the Commission's internal HR hub for payslips, leave requests and timesheets, and MyPMO, its medical reimbursement system, were brought back online earlier this week, though Sysper suffered another brief crash.Translation services: Translation tools were also disrupted this week, prompting one frustrated official to admit to “swearing a lot”, Politico reported.The severity of the breach prompted action from the Commission's top leadership. According to a leaked internal email viewed by Playbook (Politico), the Corporate Management Board (the institution's highest internal crisis-management group) held an urgent meeting earlier this month to address the “ongoing cyber incidents.”At the same time, the digital services department rolled out stricter security checks, and Tech Commissioner Henna Virkkunen updated fellow officials on the immediate response during Wednesday's College of Commissioners meeting, two officials confirmed.
Article Summary: European Commission believes it has contained most of the breach. However, investigators are still working to determine the full scope of the damage. Hackers were using ARTEX, a publicly available AI-powered tool built to spot weaknesses in IT systems. Commission temporarily pulled several applications offline as a precaution.

How Matt Eisner links the allegations to Meta’s costs

Meta shareholder Matt Eisner has sued Mark Zuckerberg . In a 656-page complaint lawsuit in federal court in Northern California this week, he named the Meta CEO and 25 others, including executives and board members. Eisner alleges that the leaders of Facebook and Instagram ’s parent company prioritised keeping users active on its platforms over protecting children and teenagers.According to a Forbes report, the complaint alleges that Meta’s leaders crafted a public account “designed to mask a systemic crisis in user engagement and growth.” Eisner says their assurances about child safety inflated Meta’s stock price, causing the company to pay more than it should have when it bought back its own shares. He filed a shareholder derivative suit seeking to recover money for Meta on the company’s behalf. Meta is named as a nominal defendant.The complaint says Meta described its recommendation system as fostering “meaningful interaction” while, Eisner alleges, “it was engineered to reward toxicity for engagement.” It also calls Meta’s 2024 proxy statement, which gives investors information ahead of shareholder votes, “materially false and misleading.” Eisner alleges that the filing misstated how Meta protected children and omitted risks the company faced if those measures fell short.ForbesInstagram head Adam Mosseri is also named in the lawsuit, which claims he prioritised “‘clicks’ over child welfare.” It says Mosseri made hiding likes optional to protect engagement, while studies show hiding counts reduced harmful social comparison.Meta’s financial filings show that it spent $25.63 billion buying back shares in the nine months through September 2021 and $26.26 billion on buybacks in 2025, including excise taxes. Those figures represent total repurchase costs. Eisner alleges that Meta overpaid because misleading statements had inflated the share price. He also points to Meta’s August 2026 agreement with 52 attorneys general to resolve litigation over teen mental health and social media. Meta says the agreement provides for payments of up to about $18.59 billion.In 2024, US District Judge Charles Breyer dismissed Eisner’s earlier case against Meta and Zuckerberg after finding that the complaint failed to adequately connect the alleged disclosure failures to an economic loss. In the new case, Eisner is asking the court to require corrective disclosures and block Meta from holding a shareholder meeting until investors receive them. 2024 dismissal order, the report noted.
